summary: Now I’m having fun! My Ramp post was really well received with one or two ‘I’m not sure what I just looked at’ comments (which is totally fair). The best I can describe what I’m doing now is exploring people and companies who are having fun with AI, doing things differently, being authentic and succ...
content: To the man with AI, everything looks like a task Subscribe Sign in To the man with AI, everything looks like a task Real* quote from Charlie Munger - lightly modernised :) Ben Tossell Nov 12, 2026 42 2 2 Share Now I’m having fun! My Ramp post was really well received with one or two ‘I’m not sure what I just looked at’ comments (which is totally fair). The best I can describe what I’m doing now is exploring people and companies who are having fun with AI, doing things differently, being authentic and succeeding . Which is basically how I want to describe my ‘work’. But I think a lot of people are living in fear. Scared they’re behind, they’re not doing enough, others using AI ‘better’ than them, where’s there job going etc. I want to focus on using AI for fun. AI is a tool, you need one agent app (I’ve been using Droid with Opus 5.5 medium, fast mode for my posts, fable here and there). Use the tool to do work beyond what you could do before, don’t think about how you can finally optimise every aspect of every little thing. (I’ve basically stopped using Grok Bot, except telling me when the tennis is on). As part of my explorations I’m working on a new post for another company I admire and who do things very differently. Coming next week… “Everyone judges a book by its cover” Can you guess which company it is? And yes, these animations are staying. Honestly I love them. I love making them too. So much so that I set up a sophisticated camera set up to monitor what my days look like and here’s the footage. Morning voice dump. Kids. Stickmen. Adobe Firefly, the AI creative studio , lets you describe what you want to create, then review the Adobe Creative Agent’s plan before it gets to work using Creative Cloud tools. You stay in control from first idea to finished result. Try it today in the Firefly Assistant! * Quick bites Anthropic is building all office software inside Claude. Latest addition: whiteboards, sheets and data . Meetings soon? Gemini 4 Carbon is out for Ultra subscribers and in the API. Also see: Gemini Decision 1 (Google’s Jev-like model) Grok Bot is now in Slack, Teams and your video calls. You can now claim your business in ChatGPT and see how often it gets mentioned. Granola now writes a nightly Agent Brief about you that any agent can read. Practical Data colours any table on the web so you can see what’s good and bad at a glance. Karri Saarinen @ karrisaarinen give a man a tool, and he'll get to work. give a man a way to build his own tools, and building tools becomes his work. 9:56 PM · Nov 11, 2026 · 26.1K Views 48 Replies · 70 Reposts · 832 Likes Jason Dainter @ jasondainter 99% AI. Hope you enjoy! summary: Is it just me or does everyone else see Ramp sponsoring everything under the sun? Over the past few years it’s like I’ve been brainwashed to think more and more about Ramp. content: How I got seduced - by Ben Tossell - Ben's Bites Subscribe Sign in How I got seduced It took them 5 years Ben Tossell Nov 10, 2026 57 8 2 Share Is it just me or does everyone else see Ramp sponsoring everything under the sun? Over the past few years it’s like I’ve been brainwashed to think more and more about Ramp. They sponsor my dreams. Rumour has it if you say ‘Ramp’ three times in a mirror, an accountant appears. To be honest, I don’t even fully know what Ramp is or does - receipts? a bank? developer tool? or a marketing stunt company? So I did some research to see how they infiltrated my brain. I turned it into a very visual, interactive page that I encourage you to look at . It’s just not the same in the email :( Ben’s Bites is brought to you by Adobe Adobe Firefly, the AI creative studio, lets you describe what you want to create, then review the Adobe Creative Agent’s plan before it gets to work using Creative Cloud tools. You stay in control from first idea to finished result. Try it today in the Firefly Assistant! Just look at that chart above. It’s crazy (1) how accurately it’s drawn and (2) how the closely related the trend of revenue, valuation, and how much they’re in my eyes and ears over time is. But their product isn’t ‘sexy’. If we look at the next super accurate chart of how hard companies have to try vs how boring their product is, we can see how Ramp and others move from the expected baseline. They get it. They have the illustrious ‘taste’ factor. They have fun with it. For example, who’s the world’s most famous accountant? Kevin from The Office (US) of course. So they did the only reasonable thing they could. Stick him in a glass box in New York and have him process 600k expense reports. 200+ Million people saw this stunt. A couple even got married in the box...wtf!? They also recognise that the ‘exhaust’ from these efforts turn into great content too. In these receipts sections ( on the live post ) you can click to see the real videos and images. Then they doubled down on Kevin (Brian), or more accurately 10x’d him by sending 9 lookalikes with him to the Super Bowl. Plus also hosted a Brian-themed party in SF where people came dressed as him with a lookalike competition where the winners got Super Bowl tickets. They sold bald caps called ‘Brian Hair’ too - reminds me of the Pitbull bald-cap mania. Oh and of course he was in the ad itself. A year before the Brians, they made their first Super Bowl ad in a week. I’ve been diving into Colossus magazine recently, they do awesome in-depth profiles of people and companies. Well worth reading. But outside of the awesome profiles I actually saw awesome display ads. I’ve never said ‘awesome display ads’ in my life, and doubt anyone else has either. But these ads were made (assuming with the help of AI) to be super personalised and unique to the content of the post itself. title: <![CDATA[Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI]]>
summary: Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here . I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1 , and it is very i...
content: Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI General, often expert, and sometimes jagged Ethan Mollick Nov 09, 2026 1,328 210 141 Share Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here . I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1 , and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers. So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is “almost” AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are. To get started I asked the new model: “I write OneUsefulThing among other stuff, I need you to create the most impressive thing I can share with people when you launch. It needs to be embeddable in a post and i can preface it however you like. it needs to have a visceral impact on people to show what you can do and the range of capabilities. It should grab them quickly. Be amazingly clever about this.” Fable asked me not to reveal anything until you had watched its video to the end. This was in one shot, with no feedback from me beyond the prompt. There is creativity here (including in the twist ending) and judgment and playfulness and cleverness. This is, I think, at the level of a human expert trying to make a movie with code alone, the sort of performance I would once have associated with AGI. The “G” in AGI Code and video creation have been areas where AI development has focused, so is Fable 5.2 really a General Intelligence? To test that, I gave the AI a variety of hard challenges in different domains: Hack some hardware from a single prompt: I have a tiny USB keyboard with a few light-up keys on my desk called a Codex Micro (ironically built to work with ChatGPT), and I asked Fable to turn it into a game console. summary: My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. content: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) My new book is out today... what happened since the last one Ethan Mollick Oct 20, 2026 813 144 69 Share My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.” Some examples of interacting with Claude to make the graphics for this post. Notice that it corrected me. “This is the worst AI you will ever use” I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence , and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI. Which company had the best AI model in the world. But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone. We are living in an exponential The data below draws on the METR Long Horizon Benchmark, which used to be the most famous chart in AI. The benchmark measured the amount of human work that an AI can do with at least a 50% chance of success from a single prompt. Gains on this benchmark have been startlingly regular. F

title: <![CDATA[The Dot and the Swarm]]>
summary: I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with...
content: The Dot and the Swarm - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Dot and the Swarm Benefitting from the Bitter Lesson Ethan Mollick Oct 01, 2026 1,404 236 143 Share I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with agents as a manager, deciding how to delegate work to agents and specifying how those agents should be organized. I thought that getting agents to work effectively as a group would take careful construction, akin to building a company, and that this would take time to figure out. Nope. I fell prey to The Bitter Lesson, the hard truth, learned over and over again, that things that we thought required elaborate human rules and thinking can be solved with the brute force of better machine learning systems and more AI. The Bitter Lesson is everywhere among AI startups and companies adopting AI. A huge amount of effort went into building elaborate computer systems to feed AIs the right information at the right time, but AI systems have learned to seek out information themselves. The same thing happened to prompting. People built elaborate templates and chains of prompts that walked the AI through a task one step at a time. Then newer models turned out to be better at planning the steps themselves, and, as our research shows , planning steps have much less value. The history of the Bitter Le— — you know what? I don’t really need to explain the Bitter Lesson, I asked Claude to do it in a music video. With one prompt, Fable wrote the lyrics and submitted it to Suno; Opus 5.5 did everything else using code alone without any image generation (How did Opus 5.5 pull this off? The Bitter Lesson tells you!). I gave no feedback at all. As somebody who teaches managers and has published research on management, I guess I believed that managing agents would be different. Humans have been working on management for a very long time without fully figuring it out. It seemed like the kind of thing that would need to be designed by people, at least for a while. It turns out that organizing work is just one more thing AI can learn to do. Which brings us to dots and Muse. Dots and Muse The number one app in the App Store right now is Meta’s Muse, a personal agent that promises to do work for you. OpenAI has now released a competitor tool, called dots. They aren’t alone: SpaceX’s Grok Bot, Instinct, and Gemini Spark all do similar things, more or less. All of these agents draw inspiration from a phenomenon you might remember from earlier this year, OpenClaw. The idea of OpenClaw and its successors, which I will call Clawlikes, is that they give an AI agent access to a computer and connect to your accounts (emails, financial records, etc.). title: <![CDATA[How big is the open model economy today?]]>
summary: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption ...
content: How big is the open model economy today? Subscribe Sign in How big is the open model economy today? Our first open model economy research note for paid subscribers. Nathan Lambert Nov 04, 2026 ∙ Paid 47 3 Share My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? Share I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents . For example, Fireworks announced at their first company conference this week that they’re serving more than 40T tokens per day to customers’ customized models. This is just one slice of their inference, a vertical that they said grew over 2x from this summer, so I would expect their total number this fall to be well above 100T tokens when we get the next update. My first instinct with these numbers has been to ground them versus any closed model or hyperscale company we can, at least in terms of token volume.
